summary: This document specifies a TLS extension letting clients send generic user mapping hints in the supplemental data handshake message from RFC 4680. An informative section defines one hint, UpnDomainHint, which a server can use to find a user in a directory database. It updates RFC 4346 and was later updated by RFC 8996.

plainLanguage.summary: When you show up at a secure door, you can also whisper a hint about who you are, like your name and company, so the guard can quickly find you in the guest list.

questions: what is the tls user mapping extension
what is the upn domain hint
how does tls map a client certificate to a user account
is a tls user mapping hint authenticated
subtitle: A TLS extension that lets a client hint which directory account its certificate belongs to.

tldr.problem: When a client authenticates to a server with a TLS certificate, the server still has to work out which user account the certificate maps to. Certificates that lack the right name, or that must map to several accounts, make this hard.
tldr.mechanism: The client and server agree on a user_mapping extension in the hello messages. The client then sends unauthenticated mapping hints in a SupplementalData handshake message before its Certificate message.
tldr.outcome: The server can use a hint to find the user's directory account, but the hint is never trusted: authentication rests solely on the client certificate. The RFC updates RFC 4346, and RFC 8996 later updated this RFC.

today: RFC 4681 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4346 and was itself updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4681 defines a TLS extension, user_mapping, and a payload for the SupplementalData handshake message from RFC 4680. Together they help a server map a client to a user account when TLS client authentication is used.

The document has a normative part (Sections 2 to 5) and an informative part (Section 6). It says that no other changes to the TLS protocol are required.
sections.plainLanguage: This document adds a small extra step to the secure-connection handshake. The visitor can pass along a hint about who they are, so the server finds the right account sooner.

sections.title: The user_mapping Extension
sections.content:
A new extension type, user_mapping(6), is added for use in both the client hello and the server hello. Its extension_data carries a UserMappingTypeList, a list of hint types.

In the client hello, the list signals the hint types the client supports. In the server hello, it signals the hint types the server prefers, and it MUST be equal to or a subset of the client's list. If the server supports none of the client's hint types, it omits the extension from its server hello.

A server that does not understand the extension simply leaves it out, and the client proceeds as normal without sending any mapping data. The hints themselves are not placed in the client hello, to avoid broadcasting them to servers that do not understand the extension.
sections.plainLanguage: First the visitor asks, "Can I tell you who I am?" If the guard says yes, they go on. If the guard does not understand the question, nothing is shared.

sections.title: User Mapping Data in the Handshake
sections.content:
RFC 4681 adds a new supplemental data type, user_mapping_data(0). Its payload is a UserMappingDataList: a vector of UserMappingData structures, each holding one hint with a type, a user_mapping_length in bytes, and the data itself.

The hints are unauthenticated. After a successful handshake, the server MAY use a hint to locate the user's account, from which user information and credentials MAY be retrieved to support authentication based on the client certificate.

The list MAY carry several hints, and their order has no meaning. If the client sends more than one, the server SHOULD use the applicable mapping it supports. Standards-track definitions of new mapping types must include a discussion of internationalization considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The hint is like a sticky note with a name on it. There can be several notes, and the guard picks one that makes sense to them.

sections.title: Message Flow
sections.content:
The client MUST include a user_mapping extension in its client hello. A server MAY reply with the extension in its server hello to say it will accept mapping data. Once both hellos carry the extension, the client MAY send a SupplementalData message containing the UserMappingDataList before its Certificate message.

The server MUST expect and gracefully handle a client that sends no SupplementalData message even after successful negotiation. The client may decide at its own discretion that its hint is no longer relevant, for example because the server certificate fails to meet certain requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides agree first, and only then does the visitor hand over the note. The visitor may also change their mind and keep the note in their pocket.

sections.title: The UPN Domain Hint
sections.content:
Section 6 is informative and describes one hint type, upn_domain_hint(64). Its UpnDomainHint structure holds a user_principal_name and a domain_name. A User Principal Name (UPN) names a user's directory entry in the form userName@domainName.

The RFC explains that relying on a UPN inside the certificate prevents using certificates without one, and requires reissuing certificates or issuing several when accounts change. With this hint, a single certificate can be mapped to one or more accounts of the user, and the certificate does not need to contain a proprietary UPN.

The domain_name field MAY be used when only domain information is needed. The user_principal_name field MAY be used to give both the user name and the domain. If both are present, the server can use whichever it chooses, and at least one MUST be non-empty. The UPN is of the form user@domain with user a UTF-8 string without "@". The domain name field is an IDN-unaware domain name slot, so names with non-ASCII characters must first be processed as described in RFC 3490.
sections.plainLanguage: The sticky note can say your full name and company, or just your company. The guard uses whichever part helps.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The hint is unauthenticated data and MUST NOT be treated as a trusted identifier. Authentication of the user MUST rely solely on validation of the client certificate. One suggested approach is to use the hint to fetch the claimed user's certificate from the trusted directory and match it against the validated client certificate from the handshake.

Because the client starts this exchange, it must decide when sending a hint is appropriate. Clients SHOULD only send the information if they recognize the server as a legitimate recipient, for instance by its name and address. If the hint itself is sensitive, the double handshake technique described in RFC 4680 can protect it.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is only a hint, so a guard must never let someone in just because of what it says. The ID card is what counts, and you should only hand your note to guards you recognize.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA created three registrations. The first is user_mapping(6) in the ExtensionType registry. The second is user_mapping_data(0) in the SupplementalDataType registry from RFC 4680. The third is a new registry for TLS UserMappingType values, whose first entry is upn_domain_hint(64).

Values 0 to 63 are assigned by Standards Action, 64 to 223 by Specification Required, and 224 to 255 are reserved for Private Use.
sections.plainLanguage: A public list keeps track of the numbers used for each kind of hint so that nobody uses the same number for two different things.
